notes.35:16: Latin 'verno tempore' ('in the springtime') is a distinctive Vulgate rendering of the Hebrew phrase for a short distance of travel.
notes.35:18: The Vulgate supplies explicit etymological glosses for both names—'that is, Son of my pain' (Filius doloris mei, for Latin Benomi) and 'that is, Son of the right hand' (Filius dextrae)—which do not appear in the Hebrew text.
notes.35:21: Latin Turrem gregis ('Tower of the Flock') translates the Hebrew place name Migdal-eder.
notes.35:29: Latin 'Consumptusque aetate' ('worn out by age') and 'appositus' ('joined' or 'placed beside') are distinctive Vulgate renderings of the Hebrew expressions 'breathed his last' and 'was gathered.'
notes.36:2: The Latin uses the feminine genitive "filiae" ("daughter") in apposition to Anah here and in 36:14 (and similarly with Matred in 36:39), even though 36:24-25 identifies Anah as a son of Zibeon.
notes.36:24: The Vulgate renders the rare Hebrew term "ha-yemim" as "aquas calidas" ("warm waters", i.e., thermal hot springs), and continues in 36:25 with "and he had a son, Dishon, and a daughter, Oholibamah".
notes.36:37: The Vulgate reads "de fluvio Rohoboth" ("from the river Rehoboth"), whereas the Hebrew has "from Rehoboth by the River"; similarly in 36:39 the Vulgate reads "Adad" (Hadad, matching 1 Chronicles 1:50) rather than the Hebrew Genesis "Hadar".
notes.36:39: The Clementine Vulgate reads 'Adar' ('Hadar', matching 25:15 and some Hebrew manuscripts) where other traditions read 'Hadad.'
notes.36:40: In this section, 36:16 reads "sons of Eliphaz" where the Hebrew has "chiefs of Eliphaz", and 36:43 reads "imperii sui" ("of their dominion") rather than "of their possession".
notes.37:2: The Vulgate reads sedecim ("sixteen") where the Hebrew Masoretic Text has "seventeen," and renders Joseph's report forensically as accusavit crimine pessimo ("accused of a most wicked crime").
notes.37:3: Latin tunicam polymitam literally means a tunic woven with many threads or colors; in 37:23 the Vulgate combines this with talari ("ankle-length"), reflecting both ancient interpretations of the garment.
notes.37:20: The Vulgate specifies cisternam veterem ("an old cistern") where the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "one of the pits."
notes.37:35: Latin in infernum ("into the underworld," literally "into the lower regions") here renders Hebrew Sheol, the abode of the dead.
notes.37:36: The Vulgate names the sellers Madianitæ ("Midianites," matching Madianitis in 37:28; cf. Hebrew Medanim), and describes Potiphar specifically as eunucho ("eunuch") and magistro militum ("commander of the soldiers/army").
notes.38:5: Reading the Hebrew place name Chezib as a verb meaning "to cease," the Vulgate renders quo nato, parere ultra cessavit ("after he was born, she ceased to give birth any further").
notes.38:12: The Vulgate identifies Hirah as opilio gregis ("shepherd of the flock") and in 38:20 as pastorem suum ("his shepherd"), reading the underlying Hebrew consonants as "shepherd" (with the Septuagint) rather than Masoretic "his friend."
notes.38:14: Latin in bivio itineris ("at the fork of the road," and in bivio in 38:21) treats the Hebrew phrase rendered in the Masoretic Text as the place name Enaim as a common noun denoting a fork in the road.
notes.38:18: Latin armillam ("bracelet," also in 38:25) renders Hebrew petil ("cord"), and Ad unum igitur coitum ("at a single union") is a distinctly concise Vulgate wording of the encounter.
notes.38:21: Clem1598-USFX reads 'in loco ista meretrix' ('that prostitute was not in the place,' or an orthographic variant for 'in loco isto,' 'in this place').
notes.38:29: Latin Quare divisa est propter te maceria? ("Why has the wall been divided because of you?") renders the Hebrew wordplay on "breach" (explaining the name Perez, Latin Phares) as a divided enclosure wall (maceria).
notes.39:1: The Vulgate renders Potiphar's titles as "eunuch" (eunuchus, matching the Septuagint against Hebrew saris, "official") and "commander of the army" (princeps exercitus, where Hebrew reads "captain of the guard").
notes.39:7: The Vulgate reads "after many days" (Post multos itaque dies), whereas the Hebrew text reads "after these things."
notes.39:13: The Vulgate distinctively specifies that Potiphar's wife saw "that she had been scorned" (et se esse contemptam), where the Hebrew states that she saw Joseph had left his garment and fled outside.
notes.39:19: The Vulgate adds the explanatory detail "overly credulous of the words of his wife" (nimium credulus verbis conjugis), a distinctly Vulgate expansion absent from the Hebrew and Septuagint.
notes.40:13: The Vulgate interprets the Hebrew idiom "lift up your head" as "remember your office/service" (recordabitur ... ministerii tui).
notes.40:16: The Vulgate reads "baskets of flour" (canistra farinæ) for the rare Hebrew term hori ("white bread" or "wickerwork"), and states that Joseph "wisely solved" (prudenter ... dissolvisset) the dream.
notes.40:19: The Vulgate distinctively renders the place of execution as "a cross" (in cruce; cf. "a gallows," in patibulo, in 40:22) and uses "tear" (lacerabunt) rather than "eat" for the birds.
notes.40:22: The Vulgate concludes with "so that the truth of the dream interpreter might be proved" (ut conjectoris veritas probaretur), where the Hebrew reads "as Joseph had interpreted to them."
notes.40:23: The Vulgate adds "with prosperity following" (succedentibus prosperis) and refers to Joseph as "his interpreter" (interpretis sui) rather than by name.
notes.41:13: The Vulgate renders the execution phrase as "in cruce" ("on a cross"), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads "on a tree."
notes.41:43: The Vulgate interprets the obscure Egyptian acclamation transliterated as "abrech" in the Hebrew text as a command "that all should bend the knee before him" ("ut omnes coram eo genu flecterent").
notes.41:45: Instead of transliterating Joseph's Egyptian name (Hebrew "Zaphenath-paneah"), the Vulgate translates it into Latin as "Salvatorem mundi" ("Savior of the world"). Like the Septuagint, the Vulgate also uses the Greek name "Heliopolis" rather than Hebrew "On" (also in 41:50).
notes.42:1: Vulgate "quare negligitis" ("Why are you negligent?") renders the Hebrew "why do you look at one another?" as a reproach for inaction.
notes.42:11: Vulgate "pacifici" ("peaceful men," also in 42:19, 31, 33) translates the Hebrew term for "honest" or "truthful men," contrasting the brothers' intentions with those of hostile spies.
notes.42:20: The Vulgate reads first-person singular "ut possim vestros probare sermones" ("so that I may be able to test your words"), rather than a passive clause ("so that your words may be verified") as in the Hebrew text.
notes.42:38: Vulgate "in terra ad quam pergitis" ("in the land to which you are going") differs from the Hebrew "on the way on which you go," and "ad inferos" ("to the underworld") renders Hebrew Sheol.
notes.43:5: Vulgate includes "ut saepe diximus" ("as we have often said"), an explanatory clause absent from the Hebrew Masoretic Text.
notes.43:10: Clem1598-USFX (with the Sixtine and Hetzenauer Clementine editions) prints 'vice alter' where feminine ablative 'vice altera' ('a second time', Codex Amiatinus) is required by the sense.
notes.43:11: Vulgate lists "resinae, et mellis, et storacis, stactes, et terebinthi, et amygdalarum" ("resin, honey, storax, stacte, terebinth, and almonds"), reflecting Jerome's identifications of several rare Hebrew plant products.
notes.43:14: Vulgate adds "meus" in "Deus autem meus omnipotens" ("my Almighty God") and renders the Hebrew expression of resignation ("if I am bereaved, I am bereaved") as "quasi orbatus absque liberis ero" ("I will be as one bereaved, without children").
notes.43:23: Vulgate "probatam ego habeo" ("I myself have [it] verified") indicates that the steward holds the brothers' payment as tested and approved, and "thesauros" ("treasures") is plural against the Hebrew singular.
notes.44:5: The Vulgate explicitly adds "that you stole" (quem furati estis) to the steward's accusation, whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text reads more generally "Is not this the one from which my lord drinks?"
notes.44:14: The Vulgate uniquely specifies that Judah entered "first" (Primusque Judas).
notes.44:18: The Clementine Vulgate links "my lord" (dominus meus) at the start of 44:19 to the end of 44:18 ("after Pharaoh, my lord"), followed by second-person "You asked" (Interrogasti), whereas the Hebrew starts 44:19 with "My lord asked his servants."
notes.44:20: The Vulgate reads "his mother has him alone" (ipsum solum habet mater sua), where the Hebrew has "he alone is left of his mother."
notes.44:28: The Vulgate uses the second person plural "and you said" (et dixistis), attributing the remark about the beast directly to the brothers rather than to Jacob himself as in the Hebrew ("and I said").
notes.45:1: The Vulgate renders the Hebrew "when Joseph made himself known to his brothers" with the distinctive Latin expression "at their mutual recognition" (agnitioni mutuæ).
notes.45:18: "The marrow of the land" (medullam terræ) literally renders the Vulgate idiom for the finest produce of Egypt, corresponding to Hebrew "the fat of the land."
notes.45:20: The Vulgate commands "Do not leave behind anything of your household goods" (Nec dimittatis quidquam de supellectili vestra), inverting the sense of the Hebrew ("Do not be concerned about your goods," i.e., do not mind leaving them).
notes.45:23: The Vulgate uniquely adds that Joseph sent Jacob "the same amount of money and clothing" (tantumdem pecuniæ et vestium) given to Benjamin.
notes.45:26: The Vulgate vividly describes Jacob's stunned reaction as "as if waking from a heavy sleep" (quasi de gravi somno evigilans), whereas the Hebrew reads "his heart grew numb."
notes.46:1: Latin Puteum juramenti ("Well of the Oath") translates Hebrew Beersheba literally (also in 46:5).
notes.46:3: Latin fortissimus Deus ("the most mighty God") translates the Hebrew divine name El as a superlative adjective rather than "God, the God of your father."
notes.46:15: Latin renders Hebrew Paddan-aram as Mesopotamia Syriæ ("Mesopotamia of Syria") and omits "to Jacob," so Latin ejus ("her") refers naturally to Leah.
notes.46:20: Latin Heliopoleos ("of Heliopolis") renders Hebrew On by its Greek name meaning "City of the Sun."
notes.46:29: Clem1598-USFX (with Sixtine 1590 and Hetzenauer 1906) prints 'curro' where fourth-declension ablative 'curru' ('chariot', Codex Amiatinus) is expected.
notes.47:2: Latin extremos ("the last" or "outermost") renders Hebrew mi-qetzeh ("from among" or "from the whole number") literally.
notes.47:13: Latin In toto enim orbe ("in the whole world") broadens Hebrew "in all the land."
notes.47:21: Latin Subjecitque eam Pharaoni, et cunctos populos ejus ("he subjected it to Pharaoh, and all its peoples") agrees with the Septuagint and Samaritan Pentateuch ("reduced to servitude") rather than the Hebrew Masoretic Text ("removed them to the cities").
notes.47:31: Latin adds Deum ("God") and conversus ("having turned"), and reads lectuli caput ("the head of the bed") with the Hebrew vocalization rather than "the top of his staff" as in the Septuagint and Hebrews 11:21.
notes.48:7: The Vulgate distinctly reads "and it was springtime" (eratque vernum tempus), whereas the Hebrew Masoretic Text refers to "some distance" still remaining to Ephrath.
notes.48:11: The Vulgate reads "I have not been deprived of the sight of you" (Non sum fraudatus aspectu tuo, agreeing with the Septuagint), whereas the Hebrew reads "I did not expect to see your face."
notes.48:15: The Vulgate reads "from my youth" (ab adolescentia mea, agreeing with the Septuagint), whereas the Hebrew reads "all my life."
notes.48:22: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew term shekhem ("ridge/shoulder" or "Shechem") as "one portion" (partem unam).
notes.49:6: The Vulgate reads "they undermined a wall" (suffoderunt murum), reading the Hebrew consonants as shur ("wall") rather than shor ("ox," as in the Masoretic Text's "they hamstrung an ox").
notes.49:10: The Vulgate renders the difficult Hebrew word shiloh as "the one who is to be sent" (qui mittendus est, linking it to shalach, "to send") and reads "the expectation of the nations" (expectatio gentium, agreeing with the Septuagint against the Hebrew "obedience of the peoples").
notes.49:22: The Vulgate translates the difficult Hebrew imagery literally in human terms ("a growing son ... handsome in appearance; the daughters ran about upon the wall"), whereas the Hebrew is commonly understood of a fruitful vine beside a spring whose branches climb over a wall.
notes.49:26: The Vulgate distinctly reads "until the desire of the eternal hills should come" (donec veniret desiderium collium æternorum, taking Hebrew ta'avah as "desire" rather than "utmost bound") and renders Hebrew nezir ("one set apart") as "Nazirite" (Nazaræi).
notes.49:31: The clause numbered 49:32 in the Hebrew Masoretic Text (stating that the field and cave were bought from the sons of Heth) is absent from the Clementine Vulgate, so native Vulgate 49:32 corresponds to Saints.Bible 49:33.
notes.50:11: The Vulgate translates the Hebrew place name Abel-mizraim into Latin as Planctus Ægypti ("Mourning of Egypt").
notes.50:13: The Vulgate translates Hebrew "the cave of the field of Machpelah" as spelunca duplici ("the double cave"), following the Septuagint and the etymology of Machpelah as "double."
notes.50:19: The Vulgate distinctly reads num Dei possumus resistere voluntati? ("Can we resist the will of God?"), whereas the Hebrew text asks "Am I in the place of God?"
notes.50:20: The Vulgate explicitly reads ut exaltaret me ("so that He might exalt me") and plural multos populos ("many peoples"), whereas the Hebrew has "to bring about as it is this day, to keep many people alive."
notes.50:22: Native Clementine Vulgate Genesis 50:22 combines Saints.Bible 50:22 and 50:23 (shifting native 50:23-25 to Saints 50:24-26). Native Vulgate Genesis 50 ends at 50:25: native 50:22 covers Saints.Bible 50:22-23, and native 50:23-25 map to Saints.Bible 50:24-26.
